takeaway: OPIMQ preserves filesystem write dependencies across multiple host and NVMe queues using per-stream epochs and FTL-delayed mappings, avoiding repeated transfer-and-flush serialization.
background: Journaling file systems must make dirty data, log records, and commit records durable in order. Traditional transfer-and-flush waits for each phase, while modern Linux and NVMe use independent per-core request queues and device command queues for parallelism.
villain: Thread migration can split one ordered epoch across queues, and journaling creates dependencies between application and journal threads. Existing barrier designs assume one queue, impose a global order, require persistent device memory, or eliminate compound transactions, sacrificing balance and concurrency.
approach: OPIMQ tags writes with stream and epoch IDs. Epoch Pinning keeps an open epoch on one request queue; a dual-stream write represents cross-thread dependencies. An order-preserving FTL flushes data freely but delays logical-to-physical mapping updates until predecessor epochs—and both siblings of a dual-stream write—are mapped.
impact: The design retains multi-core and SSD parallelism while offering ordered writes, fbarrier interfaces, and crash-consistent ext4 journaling without a persistent-memory region. It moves the durability-order contract across the filesystem, block layer, NVMe command, and FTL.

evaluation.overview: Container scaling experiments run varmail, dbench, and MySQL sysbench; fio decomposes fsync latency; further tests examine tail latency, queue balance, work stealing, CrashMonkey states, and FTL translation overhead.
evaluation.implemented: OPIMQ and OP-EXT4 on Linux 5.18.18, with ordered/barrier bio flags, two stream/epoch pairs in NVMe commands, Epoch Pinning, dual-stream writes, and an OPFTL prototype on a Cosmos OpenSSD board.
evaluation.setting: A dual-socket 40-core Dell R740XD with a 2-TB Samsung 980 Pro runs up to hundreds of Docker containers. Because that SSD lacks OPFTL, host results incorporate the 1.05% throughput cost measured separately on a 230-GB, eight-channel, single-core Cosmos board.

results.text: At 40 containers, OPIMQ reports 2.9×, 2.8×, and 2.9× the vanilla Linux/ext4 performance for varmail, dbench, and sysbench, respectively.
For a 4-KB random write followed by fsync, OPIMQ reduces mean fsync latency from 6.7 ms to 2.2 ms; across three application workloads it reduces mean fsync latency by 60.9%–69.5%.
On the Cosmos OpenSSD with five streams, OPFTL lowers throughput by 1.05% versus page mapping and leaves measured address-translation latency unchanged at 2.65 µs.

limitations: The primary Samsung SSD does not implement OPFTL, so its measured prototype penalty is injected into host experiments. The Cosmos board has one core and tests only five streams; higher-stream behavior is projected. CrashMonkey covers two workloads and 1,000 states each. The implementation changes the filesystem-to-FTL contract and assumes a stable, known following stream such as ext4's JBD.
phd_group_signal: OPIMQ identifies ordering as an end-to-end property, then assigns a precise partial-order responsibility to every I/O-stack layer. The work is instructive for crash consistency, cross-layer interfaces, queue parallelism, and device firmware co-design.

claims.text: Epoch Pinning keeps all writes in an open epoch on one request queue despite thread migration, while dual-stream writes encode one write as belonging to two ordered streams.
OPFTL may flush cache entries in any physical order but exposes them only by advancing mappings in epoch order; sibling-aware delayed mappings wait for both streams of a dual-stream write.
